column3: Its reciprocal denial of being questioned distinguishes personal accountability from the coming interrogation in the focus ayah.
It identifies affluent leaders as the recurring rejecters of a warning in a settlement, directly illuminating the focus on those indulged there.
God's measured settling and possible removal of water gives only a distant contrast to the threatened inhabitants' settled abundance.
The command to avoid listening to the Quran does not clarify flight, luxury, homes, or interrogation in the focus ayah.
The surah's opening announcement that people's reckoning has drawn near supplies the governing horizon for the later command to return for questioning.
The alternation of night and day for rest does not develop the focus narrative of a doomed town.
Its future questioning of the recipients of the reminder confirms that the focus's interrogation is answerability before God.
It establishes the nearby pattern of destroyed towns that had not believed, providing the judgment setting for the fleeing town.
It names prior indulgence as the condition behind later condemnation, though the affluent-settlement pattern is already established.
It shows people following what they were indulged in into criminality when reforming restraint is absent.
The immediately preceding sight of divine might explains why the inhabitants are running before they are ironically ordered back.
The gift of night for rest is unrelated to the reversal of fleeing inhabitants to their homes.
Its denial that later people are questioned about an earlier community supplies only a remote contrast to the focus's addressees being questioned.
The universal return to God broadly supports reversal, but adds no town, luxury, or questioning dimension.
Walking through the homes of destroyed generations makes ruined dwellings a visible warning, closely extending the focus on abandoned homes.
It repeats the same remote distinction about not being questioned for an earlier community without adding to the focus.
The surah's people hear renewed warning while playing, clarifying the heedless posture preceding the town's reckoning.
It contrasts the doomed inhabitants with a later people granted settlement in the land because they fear God's standing and warning.
Ritual purification and its concessions do not clarify the focus scene.
The near context states that God saves whom He wills and destroys the excessive, identifying the outcome surrounding the focus town.
The balanced rhythm of rest and seeking provision does not explain the inhabitants' forced return.
The covenantal command to hold revelation firmly does not add to the focus narrative.
It begins the immediate account by naming the unjust town shattered and replaced, supplying the cause and scale of the focus's disaster.
The orchard owners' exclusion of the poor does not clarify the focus ayah's luxury or interrogation.
Its command to run for healing shares the motion verb but presents a wholly different, restorative action.
Scattering and hoped-for return provide a broad reversal pattern without the focus's judicial return to homes.
It directly links the transgression of a town's affluent people to the decree and total destruction of that town.
Return to God and full recompense gives the focus's questioning an explicit eschatological accountability horizon.
The same surah portrays unjust hearers as distracted and privately dismissive, filling out the denial that precedes their punishment.
Punishment seizing the affluent and reducing them to cries closely parallels the sudden collapse of the focus town's comfort.
Rules on expiating deliberate oaths do not explain the focus's interrogation.
The immediate sequel shows their cry ending only when they become a harvested, extinguished remnant, completing the focus scene.
God's ownership of all that settles by night and day offers only a general contrast to the inhabitants' claimed security in homes.
Its final return and disclosure of disputes give only a general accountability parallel.
The mortality of messengers contributes a limited same-surah reminder of transience, not the town's judgment.
The changing shadow does not clarify flight, return, luxury, or questioning.
The legal instruction not to return emigrant women to disbelievers is unrelated to the focus's coerced return.
Creation not being purposeless and return to God supports the judicial force of the focus's summons back.
Nightly rest and daylight activity do not develop the ruined-settlement scene.
Its terse declaration of return to the Lord reinforces the direction of ultimate answerability in the focus.
God's knowledge of every utterance in heaven and earth supplies a limited basis for the focus's coming questioning.
Marital tranquility does not clarify the threatened inhabitants' dwellings.
Instructions on modesty do not add to the focus narrative.
The judgment over grazing damage shares a legal sense of judgment but not the focus's destruction scene.
The possibility of stilling the wind offers only a distant image of divinely arrested movement.
Directions for charitable spending do not clarify the focus ayah.
The same surah's catalog of dismissive reactions supplies limited background to the town's unbelief.
It extends the affluent elite's refusal by showing how inherited custom protects their social order against warning.
Failure to feed the poor does not illuminate the focus's return to luxury and homes.
Ibrahim's plan concerning idols does not add to the focus scene.
The ark's tranquility and inherited relics do not clarify the focus ayah.
The concrete condition of an impoverished person does not clarify the focus's affluent inhabitants.
Repeated destruction of generations confirms divine knowledge of sin, but is less specific than the earlier town parallels.
It joins arrogant enjoyment of livelihood to destruction and nearly uninhabited homes, closely matching both luxury and dwellings in the focus.
The sky's returning rain does not clarify the focus narrative.
Its instruction to ask those with knowledge is a different use of questioning, with only same-surah proximity.
Not urging food for the poor does not explain the focus's judgment on an affluent town.
Building as though one will live forever offers a limited parallel to false permanence in prosperous dwellings.
Nuh's rescue and the drowning of deniers do not add a distinct reading to the focus town's fate.
Abundant dwelling is made conditional by a boundary; crossing it destabilizes residence, a useful contrast to indulgence without restraint.
The righteous command to eat and drink pleasantly is not tied to the focus's condemned luxury.
The book containing the audience's reminder gives only broad same-surah warning context.
Cosmic cycles of night and day do not develop the focus scene.
Entry into Paradise in joy does not clarify the doomed town.
God's knowledge of open and hidden speech adds no distinct connection beyond the earlier accountability context.
It reiterates ruined generations' homes as warning, but adds little beyond the earlier, closer dwelling parallel.
The instruction not to weaken or call for peace does not clarify the focus ayah.
The same surah's testing by good and evil and return to God broadens the focus's disaster into a stated pattern of trial and return.
Settlement in the land is real but temporary before a final gathering, qualifying any confidence in dwelling as a final refuge.
Returning to themselves is an inward recognition scene, only distantly echoing the focus's commanded return.
Addressing the erring deniers does not add to the focus's affluent-town scene.
It presents a well-provisioned settlement and its dwellings as divine gift, establishing the positive condition whose misuse the focus reverses.
Encouragement after defeat does not clarify the focus narrative.
A lasting word among descendants oriented to return provides only a remote return motif.
Marital rest does not clarify the return to homes under judgment.
A commanded return from a house is voluntary etiquette, providing only a contrast to the focus's ironic coercion.
Persistence in grave sin does not add a distinct account of the focus town.
Abundant residence is paired with humble entry and seeking forgiveness, a direct counterpattern to secure, unrestrained dwelling.
The Prophet's grief over plotters does not clarify the focus ayah.
Withholding provision from the poor is only an indirect ethical contrast to the privileged town's abundance.
Feeding vulnerable people does not clarify the focus's reversal of affluent fugitives.
Revival after death does not add to the focus narrative.
Withholding small assistance supplies only a distant contrast to the focus's abundance in homes.
Inner tranquility overcoming zeal does not clarify the focus's external flight and judgment.
The command not to exalt oneself above God lacks a distinct link to the focus scene.
Homes as God-given shelter modestly contrasts with treating dwellings and luxury as secure possessions.
Repentance linked with increased rain and strength gives only a general alternative to criminal indulgence.
It repeats the conditional abundance-and-dwelling pattern already supplied by 2:35, without adding much.
Deceptive hopes lasting until God's command provide a broad caution against false security before judgment.
Tranquility placed in believers' hearts does not illuminate the focus's doomed inhabitants.
Its statement that the messenger is not questioned about Hell's people gives a limited contrast to the focus addressees' questioning.
The inability of false gods to hear a call does not clarify the focus's interrogation.
God's provision for creatures does not explain the focus's punished luxury.
It shows a person forgetting God after receiving favor and being told to enjoy disbelief only briefly, directly qualifying luxury as temporary and culpable.
The adornment of worldly life and its reversal at resurrection gives a broad, less specific contrast to privileged security.
Comparative communal hostility does not clarify the focus ayah.
The request for a heavenly table does not develop the focus scene.
The question about death does not clarify the focus's interrogation.
God's living self-subsistence does not add a focused connection.
The description of revelation's source does not clarify the focus ayah.
The fugitives' confession, "we were wrongdoers," is the immediate answer to the focus's ironic return and anticipated questioning.
It gives the recurring pattern of a town struck by divine punishment while its people are at rest, framing the focus town's sudden collapse.
Its only cry after punishment, admitting wrongdoing, closely parallels the focus passage's ensuing confession of guilt.
Opened abundance followed by sudden seizure and despair sharply clarifies how ease can precede irreversible judgment.
It states that earlier generations were destroyed for wrongdoing after rejecting clear messengers, supplying the warning-and-destruction pattern.
God's seizure of wrongdoing towns is painful and severe, directly clarifying the force behind the focus inhabitants' flight.
A secure, tranquil town with abundant provision becomes hungry and fearful after ingratitude, closely reversing the focus's privileged dwelling.
It universalizes the prospect that towns face destruction or severe punishment before the Day of Resurrection.
It explicitly connects the destruction of towns to wrongdoing and an appointed term, giving the focus judgment a measured finality.
It names people and ancestors allowed enjoyment until life became prolonged, explaining the complacent extension behind the focus's luxury.
The prohibition on a destroyed town returning adds a grave boundary to the focus's commanded return: return to homes is not restoration.
It says no town was destroyed without warners, locating the focus catastrophe within prior warning rather than arbitrary ruin.
It declares that prolonged enjoyment cannot benefit people once punishment comes, directly qualifying the focus's enjoyed prosperity.
God does not destroy towns until sending a messenger in their center, completing the focus's warning, accountability, and destruction sequence.
The destruction of Saba after its prosperous settlement turns the provision-and-dwelling scene into a concrete counterpart to the focus's reversal.
The arrogant strength of 'Ad and its rejection of signs show a community's self-assured power immediately before the punishment detailed next.
A devastating wind in days of disaster gives a direct example of a proud, prosperous people made to taste humiliating punishment.
The abandoned gardens, springs, treasures, noble dwellings, and comfortable life are an especially close image of luxury and homes left behind under judgment.
Its invitation to see the end of earlier deniers makes destroyed communities a continuing warning, like the focus town's fate.
The expulsion of a people from their homes overturns their expectation of security and makes dwellings themselves evidence of divine judgment.
Towns rebelling against God's command are subjected to severe reckoning and punishment, directly joining civic wrongdoing with interrogation.
